titleStmt.title: Outline for Meeting With the Secretary on Japanese Peace Setlement

head.hi: Outline for Meeting With the Secretary on Japanese Peace Setlement

div.p: A course of action for the U.S. Government with respect to a Japanese peace settlement; and
A procedure by which agreement within the U.S. Government to such a course of action can be reached.
I. Conclusion of an “Agreement on the Restoration of Normal Political and Economic Relations with Japan” while continuing unchanged the occupation arrangements with respect to security matters.

list.item: Would minimize political and military risks involved in proceeding without USSR and China, while at same time establishing more stable political relationships with respect to Japan.
Friendly Allies in Far East would not be forced openly to choose sides between U.S. and USSR on military issue.
Japanese Government would be less vulnerable (than under II) to Communist propaganda that it had sold out Japanese people to Western imperialism.
Substantially satisfies primary concerns of JCS concerning effects of separate peace treaty on U.S. security.

The co-existence of legal state of war and of normal political and economic relations with Japan and rather substantial nature of change in Allied occupation controls would be seized upon by USSR and Chinese Communists in charges that agreement is subterfuge and that United States and other signatory powers had violated their wartime agreements with USSR and China.
Japan’s desire for total termination of occupation would be disappointed.

div.p: II. Conclusion of a Peace Treaty which authorizes the maintenance of U.S. or Western-Allied bases in Japan.

list.item: Would be more clean-cut than Course I.

Because of strong Japanese desire for peace treaty and likely acceptance of U.S. forces as best available solution of Japan’s security problem, would take advantage of unique opportunity which may not again recur to secure exclusive long-term U.S. or Western Allied bases in Japan.
Would completely satisfy Japan’s desire for a peace treaty.
Would from legal standpoint, if UN approval is obtained, provide broadest international basis for U.S. security forces in Japan.
Would commit U.S. to long-term pattern of political relationships based on Japan’s consent to U.S. bases and nakedly military U.S. posture in Japan.
Would result in break with USSR and Chinese Communists over issue of U.S. bases in Japan.
Would confront friendly Far East Allies with necessity for open choice of sides in East-West conflict on a military issue.

USSR and Chinese Communists would make greatest possible difficulties for Japanese Government, which would be subjected to all-out propaganda campaign of having sold out Japanese people to Western imperialism.
Complete termination of SCAP controls might increase Soviet and Chinese Communist capabilities of increasing their influence over Japan.
If UN consideration is sought, might well deepen issue dividing U.S. and USSR with possible harm to United Nations itself.
